title: Coal Genesis, Rank & Macerals
subtitle: Peat to anthracite: heat, pressure, time

stages.title: Coal is cooked plant matter
stages.text: A Jharia seam and a Neyveli lignite started as the same swamp. One was cooked far longer and hotter. | Plant debris accumulates as peat; burial converts it to coal in two steps — biochemical (bacteria, near surface) then geochemical (heat and pressure, at depth). | Rank measures how far that cooking went: volatiles and moisture fall, carbon and reflectance rise. | Seam at burial depth | Geothermal gradient | Anthracite end-member | Vitrinite reflectance Ro | Drift vs in-situ origin? | What are macerals? | Why does moisture fall with rank?

stages.title: How metal gets concentrated
stages.text: A copper mine is profitable at 0.5 % Cu, yet average crust holds about 0.005 %. Something concentrated it a hundredfold. | Ore is ordinary crustal metal concentrated hundreds of times by a geological process: magma crystallisation, hot fluids, sedimentation or weathering. | In supergene enrichment, rain leaches metal from the oxidised top and re-deposits it just below the water table. | Leached cap / gossan | Water table = redox boundary | Enriched blanket | Hypogene (primary) ore | The four genetic families with Indian examples? | Why does pyrite matter?

title: True vs Apparent Dip
subtitle: Strike, dip and every section in between

stages.title: A seam dips most steeply in one direction only
stages.text: Drive a gallery one way along a dipping seam and it stays dead level; turn 90° and it climbs as steeply as the bed itself. | Strike is the horizontal line on a bed; true dip is the steepest slope, measured at right angles to strike. | Any other section through the bed shows a smaller, apparent dip — zero along strike. | Strike line | True dip direction | Section line at angle β | Apparent dip in section | Where does tan α = tan δ·sin β come from? | Why do Indian mines talk of '1 in 4'?

title: Faults: Throw, Heave, Gap & Overlap
subtitle: Finding the seam on the other side

stages.title: Faults move the seam — geometry tells you where
stages.text: The coal face suddenly hits stone. Is the seam above you or below? The fault's tilt already tells you. | In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down (extension); in a reverse or thrust fault it moves up (compression). | Throw is the vertical offset; heave is the horizontal one. Normal faults leave a barren gap in plan; reverse faults create an overlap with the seam repeated. | Fault plane | Footwall seam | Displaced seam | Heave in plan | Why do normal faults form? | Why are faults hazardous underground? | Strike-slip faults?

title: Diamond Core Drilling & RQD
subtitle: Reading rock quality from the core box

stages.title: The core box is the rock's report card
stages.text: Two boreholes, same rock type: one core comes up in metre-long sticks, the other as gravel. Only one will stand as an open roof. | Diamond drilling recovers intact cylinders of rock; the logger records lithology, recovery and fracture spacing. | RQD — the percentage of a run made of sound pieces ≥ 10 cm — is the fastest index of rock-mass quality and feeds RMR and Q. | Sound piece ≥ 10 cm | Broken zone | Core recovery | Why exactly 10 cm? | Drilling-induced breaks? | No core? stages.title: Three questions decide whether it's a reserve
stages.text: A rich, well-drilled deposit can still be 'only a resource' if nobody has shown it pays to mine. | India's UNFC system (MEMC Rules 2015) codes every deposit on three axes: Economic viability (E), Feasibility study level (F) and Geological assurance (G). | Only E1 material with a feasibility (F1) or prefeasibility (F2) study and good geology (G1/G2) is a Mineral Reserve; everything else is a Resource. | E axis | F axis | G axis | Code | Why separate reserve from resource? | Cross-section method?

title: Access Selection & Shaft Pillars
subtitle: Adit vs incline vs vertical shaft

stages.title: Depth decides the door
stages.text: A seam 40 m below a hillside needs no hoist at all, while the same seam under a plain might need a 600 m shaft. | Where a seam outcrops above drainage, an adit gives gravity drainage and no hoisting. Shallow seams are opened by belt inclines; deep ones by vertical shafts. | Incline length grows as depth ÷ sin(gradient), so beyond a few hundred metres the shorter shaft wins despite its winder. | Belt incline | Vertical shaft | Seam horizon | Capital comparison | Why do inclines lose at depth? | What is a shaft pillar? | Angle of draw?

title: Shaft Sinking Cycle & the Galloway Stage
subtitle: Drill, blast, muck, line — repeat

stages.title: Sinking is a cycle — the slowest step sets the pace
stages.text: Speed up drilling all you like: if mucking takes half the cycle, the shaft still sinks no faster. | Conventional sinking repeats drilling, charging-blasting-ventilating, mucking by cactus grab into kibbles, and concrete lining. | A multi-deck Galloway stage, hung on winch ropes, lets lining proceed from upper decks while the bottom is drilled and mucked. | Galloway stage | Kibble | Mucking bottleneck | Advance rate | Why line concurrently? | Why a swell factor?

unitTitle: Mine Development: Access, Shaft Sinking & Drivage
title: Special Sinking: Freezing & Cementation
subtitle: Sinking through water-bearing ground

stages.title: Turn the aquifer into a temporary wall
stages.text: Dig into running sand and the hole fills as fast as you empty it, so sinkers freeze the ground solid first. | Running sand and fissured aquifers cannot be sunk conventionally — water and fines flow into the excavation. | Freezing circulates cold brine (or liquid nitrogen) through a ring of boreholes, creating a frozen cylinder that is both watertight and load-bearing; cementation instead injects grout ahead to seal fissures. | Shaft excavation | Frozen wall | Freeze holes | Ground + water pressure | Why Lamé? | Cementation vs freezing? | Liquid nitrogen?

unitTitle: Mine Development: Access, Shaft Sinking & Drivage
title: Drift Drill-and-Blast: the Burn Cut
subtitle: Creating a free face where there is none

stages.title: No free face? Make one
stages.text: Rock breaks easily toward open space, and a drift face has none. The first holes must make their own. | A drift face is confined on all sides, so the first holes must blast into an empty, large-diameter relief hole. | Each delay then breaks toward the opening the previous one created: cut → easers → perimeter → lifters. | Empty relief hole | Perimeter (contour) holes | Lifters | Pull | Why does relief-hole diameter limit depth? | Burn cut vs V-cut?

unitTitle: Mine Development: Access, Shaft Sinking & Drivage
title: Mechanical Excavation: Roadheaders, CMs & TBMs
subtitle: Cutting mechanics and specific energy

stages.title: Cutting is an energy budget
stages.text: A roadheader that glides through shale can stall on sandstone twice as strong: every MPa costs cutting energy. | Picks and disc cutters break rock by indentation and chip formation; the energy spent per cubic metre is the specific energy (SE). | SE rises with rock strength, so cutting rate = useful power ÷ SE falls in hard rock — each machine has a strength envelope. | Rock strength | TBM envelope | Machine | Instantaneous cutting rate | Why is drag-pick cutting limited in hard rock? | Raise boring vs blind shaft boring?

unitTitle: Mine Development: Access, Shaft Sinking & Drivage
title: Development Engineer's Board
subtitle: Access, sinking and drivage under fire

stages.title: An opening diverts the stress flow
stages.text: Cut a round hole in loaded rock and the walls carry up to three times the stress the rock carried before. | Rock carries vertical stress from overburden and horizontal stress from confinement and tectonics (ratio K = σh/σv). | Cutting a hole forces those stress 'flow lines' around it, concentrating them on the boundary — up to 3× in the sidewalls of a circular opening. | Roof (crown) | Sidewalls | Far-field stresses | Failure map | Elastic, plastic, viscoelastic — which applies? | Where does horizontal stress come from? | Why only up to 3?

stages.title: Confinement makes rock stronger
stages.text: A rock that crumbles in your hand can carry enormous loads deep underground, because squeezing it from the sides makes it stronger. | Mohr–Coulomb treats strength as cohesion plus friction on a shear plane — a straight line in σ1–σ3 space. | Hoek–Brown, fitted to real rock-mass behaviour, curves: strength gains fast at low confinement and flattens as cracks close; GSI scales it from intact rock to a jointed mass. | Hoek–Brown envelope | Mohr–Coulomb line | Working confinement | What did Griffith add? | Brittle vs ductile? | Why is GSI so influential?

title: Rock Mass Classification: RMR, Q, GSI
subtitle: Turning a core box into a support design

stages.title: Five numbers rate a rock mass
stages.text: Strong rock full of wet, slickensided joints can be weaker roof than mediocre rock with tight, dry ones. | RMR adds ratings for intact strength, RQD, joint spacing, joint condition and groundwater, then adjusts for joint orientation. | Q multiplies block size, inter-block shear strength and active stress; GSI feeds Hoek–Brown. All three translate geology into support classes. | Rating stack | Classes I–V | Support guidance | What is Q? | RMR ↔ Q ↔ GSI?

title: Roof Bolting: Suspension & Beam Building
subtitle: Beam theory of a stratified roof

stages.title: Thin layers sag; clamped layers span
stages.text: Five thin shale layers sag like loose pages; bolt them into one beam and the same roof spans the gallery. | A laminated roof behaves like a stack of thin beams: each carries its own weight, and bending stress grows with span² and falls with thickness. | Bolts either suspend the weak layer from strong strata above, or clamp the laminae so they act as one thick beam — beam building. | Laminated immediate roof | Anchorage horizon | Span | Pillar rib | Where does σ = γL²/(2t) come from? | Pressure arch theory? | Plate vs beam?

title: Pillar Design: Tributary Area & Strength Formulae
subtitle: Salamon–Munro and CMRI workbench

stages.title: A pillar carries its share of the roof
stages.text: Widen the galleries by a metre and every pillar in the panel quietly picks up extra load. | Tributary area theory: each pillar supports the overburden over its own area plus half the surrounding galleries. | Pillar strength falls as height rises and grows with width — so the width-to-height ratio is the heart of pillar design. | Tributary area | Gallery | Strength formula | Factor of safety | Why does height weaken pillars? | Why does CMRI's formula include depth? | Statutory pillar sizes?

title: Opencast Slope Stability
subtitle: Plane, wedge, circular and toppling failure

stages.title: A slope fails along its weakest path
stages.text: A slope can stand for years and then slide in one monsoon night: water lifts the block off its friction. | Plane failure needs a discontinuity that daylights in the face (dips flatter than the face) and steeper than its friction angle. | The factor of safety compares resisting forces (cohesion + friction) with driving forces along that plane — and water attacks the friction term. | Sliding block | Failure plane | Crest | Pit floor | Wedge failure? | Circular failure? | Toppling? | How does water reduce FOS?

stages.title: Extraction reaches the surface as a trough
stages.text: Houses a kilometre from the panel can crack, because extraction spreads upward and outward as it reaches the surface. | Caving above an extracted panel propagates upward and appears at surface as a subsidence trough bounded by the angle of draw. | Narrow (sub-critical) panels are bridged and subside less; at critical width the full subsidence a·m develops at the centre. | Extracted panel | Angle of draw | Trough | Smax | Why do strains matter more than subsidence? | Rockburst vs coal bump?

stages.title: Every drill is an energy delivery system
stages.text: The same hammer drill that flies through the first 6 m crawls at 30 m: energy leaks out at every rod coupling. | Percussive drills crush rock under the bit by impact and chip it as the bit indexes round; rotary drills crush or shear it under thrust and torque. | Penetration rate is simply the power that reaches the rock divided by the energy needed per cubic metre — so where the hammer sits matters. | Top-hammer | Rod couplings | Penetration comparison | Energy at the bit | How does a percussive bit break rock? | Why does rotary drilling struggle in hard rock? | Dust from drilling?

stages.title: An explosive is a fast, self-supplied fire
stages.text: Blast with too much fuel oil and the cloud turns to CO; too little and you breathe orange NOx. | Explosives carry their own oxygen: in ANFO, ammonium nitrate supplies O and fuel oil supplies C and H. | Detonation is a supersonic shock front sustained by the reaction behind it; deflagration is subsonic burning — far weaker and fume-rich. | Oxygen balance | Detonation front | Post-blast fumes | Impedance matching | Deflagration vs detonation? | Why ρ·VOD²/4? | Permitted explosives?

title: Fragmentation: Kuz-Ram Blast Optimiser
subtitle: Shock vs gas, burden, spacing and powder factor

stages.title: Shock cracks, gas heaves
stages.text: Most rock in a blast is not broken by the bang but by tension, the shock wave bouncing back off the free face. | The detonation shock crushes the borehole wall and drives radial cracks; reflected tensile waves from the free face spall the burden. | Gas pressure then wedges into the cracks and heaves the broken burden — fragment size depends on how much energy each tonne receives. | Explosive column | Stemming | Size distribution | Oversize | Why does powder factor dominate? | What controls uniformity n? | Rock factor A?

title: Delay Timing, NONEL Sequencing & Misfires
subtitle: The firing wave and the cut-off trap

stages.title: Timing turns many holes into a controlled sequence
stages.text: Fire 50 holes at once and you shake the village; fire them 25 ms apart and the same charge breaks rock gently. | Delays let each hole break toward the free face created by the one before it, and keep the charge per delay — and therefore vibration — low. | In NONEL systems the surface signal must reach every hole before ground movement from the first detonation can sever the tubes: long in-hole, short surface delays. | Initiation point | Surface connector | Cut-off risk | Detonation times | Why long in-hole delays? | Electronic detonators? | Common misfire causes?

stages.title: Vibration falls with scaled distance
stages.text: Move the blast twice as far from the village and you can fire roughly four times the charge per delay: vibration follows scaled distance. | Peak particle velocity depends on distance and the charge per delay: V = K(D/√Q)^−b. | DGMS limits PPV by structure type and dominant frequency — low frequencies resonate with buildings and get the tightest limits. | Attenuation curve | Structure | Permissible limit | Danger zone | Why √Q? | Flyrock causes? | Airblast?

subtitle: Design it, time it, fire it safely

title: Pit Geometry & Stripping Ratio
subtitle: How deep can the pit economically go?

stages.title: Every tonne of coal carries its waste
stages.text: The first tonnes of coal in a pit cost little waste; the last tonnes at depth can carry ten times more. | The stripping ratio is waste moved per tonne of coal; it grows quickly with depth because the pit widens at the surface as the walls lean back. | The pit is economic while the stripping ratio stays below the break-even stripping ratio — the waste one tonne's margin can pay to remove. | Overburden wedge | Coal | Overall slope | SR vs BESR | Overall vs instantaneous stripping ratio? | Bench geometry?

title: Dragline Cut-and-Cast & Excavator Envelopes
subtitle: Rope shovels, hydraulic excavators, draglines, BWEs, surface miners

stages.title: A dragline digs and dumps in one swing
stages.text: A dragline moves overburden without a single truck, but only if the spoil fits within its reach. | Standing on the highwall, a dragline digs the overburden cut and side-casts it into the previous void — no trucks needed. | Its reach must cover the spoil pile's centre; when the spoil geometry outgrows the reach, material must be rehandled (extended-bench methods). | Overburden cut | Spoil pile | Dragline | Exposed coal | Rope shovel vs hydraulic excavator? | Bucket-wheel excavators and surface miners? | Extended bench?

stages.title: Shovel and trucks are one machine
stages.text: Buy one truck too many and it idles in the queue; one too few and a crore-rupee shovel waits. | The match factor compares the rate trucks arrive with the rate the shovel can load them: MF = 1 is a balanced fleet. | Below 1 the shovel waits (lost production); above 1 trucks queue (lost capital). Haul distance and passes per truck drive the balance. | Loading unit | Loaded haul | Dump | Match factor | Why not just add trucks? | Why 3–5 passes?

stages.title: Light vehicle in the blind spot

title: Haul Road Physics & Design
subtitle: Rolling resistance, grade, rimpull, retarders, curves

stages.title: Every percent of resistance is paid in speed
stages.text: A loaded truck on a 10 % ramp is fighting the equivalent of an extra 100 kg for every tonne it carries. | A truck must overcome rolling resistance (tyre and road deformation) plus grade resistance — each roughly 10 kg per tonne per percent. | Rimpull × speed = power, so on a ramp, total resistance fixes the speed; on downgrades the retarder must absorb the energy. | Truck on ramp | Ramp gradient | Curve | Total resistance | What sets rolling resistance? | Why retarders? | Road width and berms?

stages.title: A dump is a loose slope that never stops settling
stages.text: A dump looks stable because each bench does, but it is the overall slope from crest to toe that fails. | Each deck stands at the spoil's angle of repose; berms between decks flatten the overall slope that actually governs stability. | Water (pore pressure) and weak foundations (black cotton soil, paddy fields) are behind most Indian dump failures. | Deck face | Berm | Overall slope | Factor of safety | Why do dumps fail in the monsoon? | Foundation preparation? | Reclamation?

title: Bord & Pillar Depillaring & Goaf Behaviour
subtitle: Caving, stowing, main falls and air blast

stages.title: Depillaring hands the load to the goaf edge
stages.text: Pull the last stook and the roof does not wait: kilometres of rock overhead must find somewhere new to rest. | In development, pillars share the overburden evenly; in depillaring, extracted areas transfer load to the goaf edge and the remaining stooks. | Weak immediate roof caves and bulks to fill the void; a strong main roof can hang over a large area and then fall at once — driving an air blast through the workings. | Solid / pillars | Immediate caving | Main roof | Goaf-edge supports | Caving vs hydraulic sand stowing? | Why do air blasts happen? | Thick-seam methods?

stages.title: When will the main roof break?
A longwall carries the roof on a moving wall of shields
stages.text: A longwall is a 250 m tunnel that walks forward every shift, holding up the roof with hydraulic legs. | The overburden that once rested on the extracted coal is redistributed: a front abutment builds ahead of the face and a rear abutment where the goaf recompacts. | Shields must hold the detached roof block between face and goaf, then yield and advance every web cut by the shearer. | Front abutment | Powered shield | Shearer & AFC | Goaf | What is the detached block model? | Why yield rather than rigid supports? | Tip-to-face distance?

stages.title: Every metre of slough dilutes the ore
stages.text: Every tonne of wall rock that sloughs into a stope is mined, hauled and milled for nothing. | Stoping methods range from unsupported (sublevel open stoping, VCR, shrinkage) through supported (cut-and-fill, square-set) to caving. | Dilution — waste mixed with ore — is driven by hanging-wall overbreak (ELOS) relative to ore width, so narrow veins suffer most. | Orebody | Hanging-wall slough | Diluted grade | Unsupported methods? | Supported methods? | Why is dilution so costly?

stages.title: Ore flows to a drawpoint in an ellipsoid
stages.text: In a block cave you never touch the ore with a drill; you just keep pulling broken rock from below and gravity does the rest. | Undercut a large block and it caves under gravity; broken ore is pulled from drawpoints at the extraction level. | Material reporting to one drawpoint comes from an elongated ellipsoid. If neighbouring ellipsoids overlap, the column lowers evenly; if not, waste races down early and ore is left behind. | Isolated draw zone | Drawpoint | Overlying waste | Why interactive draw? | Draw control?

stages.title: Fire in the goaf, stowing proposed
Know where each gas hides and what it does
stages.text: Methane hugs the roof, CO₂ pools in the sump and CO has no smell at all, so each one ambushes you in a different place. | Methane is lighter than air and layers at the roof; CO₂ is heavier and pools on the floor; CO kills invisibly by binding haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen. | Methane only explodes inside a window of both fuel and oxygen — Coward's triangle maps it, including mixtures that become explosive when fresh air is added. | Explosive zone | Lower explosive limit | Nose | Air-dilution line | Why is CO so toxic? | How does methane layering form? | Other gases?

stages.title: Airflow obeys a square law
stages.text: Ask a fan for twice the air and it must push four times the pressure: airways fight back with the square of the flow. | Friction in airways makes pressure loss grow with the square of airflow: P = RQ², where resistance R depends on roughness, perimeter, length and area³. | In a network, flow divides so every parallel path has the same pressure drop (Kirchhoff); regulators add resistance to steer air where it is needed. | Main fan | Junction (Kirchhoff I) | Regulator | District split | Why area cubed? | Equivalent orifice? | Statutory quantity?

stages.title: The fan runs where its curve meets the mine's
stages.text: Add a door or a collapse to the mine and the fan quietly delivers less air; it always runs where two curves cross. | The fan characteristic (pressure vs flow) intersects the mine resistance curve P = RQ² at the operating point. | Axial fans have a stall zone left of their pressure peak — operate there and flow oscillates violently. Heat differences between shafts add a natural ventilation pressure. | Stall zone | Pressure peak | Mine curve | Operating point | Centrifugal vs axial? | Where does NVP come from? | Fan laws?

title: Psychrometry & Heat Stress
subtitle: Wet bulb, humidity and statutory heat limits

stages.title: Heat kills through the wet bulb
stages.text: 34 °C in dry air is hard work; 34 °C in saturated air can kill, because sweat stops cooling you. | The body sheds heat mainly by evaporating sweat; humid air (high wet-bulb temperature) stops evaporation no matter what the dry bulb says. | Indian coal mine regulations therefore set limits on wet-bulb temperature: above 30.5 °C the face needs at least 1 m/s air, and above 33.5 °C no one may work. | Dry bulb | Wet bulb | Statutory lines | Air velocity | Why does depth heat the air? | Psychrometer equation? | Heat stroke first aid?

stages.title: Coal can set itself on fire
stages.text: A coal pile can catch fire with no spark at all; it just has to make heat faster than the air carries it away. | Coal oxidises at room temperature; when heat from oxidation exceeds heat lost to ventilation, temperature climbs and the reaction accelerates — self-heating. | Gas ratios built on oxygen deficiency detect heating early, independent of dilution by fresh air. | Graham's ratio | Sample composition | Jones–Trickett ratio | What makes coal prone? | Crossing point temperature? | Controls?

title: Coal Dust Explosions & Stone Dusting
subtitle: Propagation physics and the heat-sink defence

stages.title: A small firedamp ignition can raise a dust cloud
stages.text: A small firedamp flash can turn a roadway of settled coal dust into a cloud, and the cloud into a mine-wide explosion. | A methane ignition's pressure wave lifts settled coal dust; the flame then burns through that cloud, raising more dust ahead of it — a self-propagating explosion. | Stone dust is inert: mixed into roadway dust, it absorbs heat (heat sink) and dilutes fuel so the flame cannot sustain itself. | Settled dust | Raised cloud | Incombustible content | Why does stone dust work? | Barriers?

stages.title: A pump must lift water — and must not boil it

stages.title: Liberation costs energy — mostly at the fine end
stages.text: Crushing rock from boulders to sand is cheap; grinding it from sand to flour is where the mill power bill goes. | Minerals must be broken small enough to free (liberate) valuable grains from gangue before they can be separated. | Energy per tonne rises steeply as product size falls: Bond's law scales it with 1/√size, between Kick (coarse) and Rittinger (fine). | Feed F80 | Product P80 | Ball mill | Bond equation | Rittinger vs Kick vs Bond? | Why not grind everything ultra-fine?

stages.text: Drop coal and shale into a liquid of the right density and the coal floats while the shale sinks. | Gravity and dense-medium separation use density; settling speed follows Stokes' law for fines and Newton's law for coarse particles. | Coal washability (float–sink) data tell you, for any cut-point, how much clean coal you get and at what ash — and how hard the coal is to wash. | Washability curve | Ash target | Operating point | Near-gravity material? | Flotation surface chemistry? | Hindered settling?

title: Mine Electricals: Earthing, FLP & IS
subtitle: Restricted neutral, earth leakage, flameproof and intrinsic safety

stages.title: Limit the fault, then make sparks harmless
stages.text: A spark from a faulty cable can ignite methane; the trick is to keep the fault current too small to spark and cut it in milliseconds. | Underground coal systems earth the transformer neutral through a resistor so an earth fault draws only a small current (commonly limited to 750 mA) — and an earth-leakage relay trips it fast. | Where firedamp may be present, apparatus is flameproof (FLP: contains an internal explosion and cools escaping gases in narrow flame paths) or intrinsically safe (IS: circuit energy too low to ignite methane). | Transformer | Neutral earthing resistor | Earth fault | Ea

title: Koepe Winding & Haulage Safety Devices
subtitle: Friction drives, overwinds and runaways

stages.title: A Koepe wheel lifts by friction alone
stages.text: A Koepe winder has no drum to wind rope on; the skips are lifted by friction alone, and friction has a limit. | The rope passes over the friction wheel; motion depends on the tension ratio staying within Euler's capstan limit, T₁/T₂ ≤ e^(μθ). | Acceleration, braking, payload and an unbalanced rope push the ratio up; slip is prevented by mass, friction lining and wrap — and every winder needs overwind, overspeed and arresting protection. | Friction wheel | Tight side T₁ | Loaded skip | Tail rope | Detaching hooks? | Winder protection? | Rope haulage devices?

title: Discounted Cash Flow & Indian Mineral Levies
subtitle: NPV, IRR, payback, royalty, DMF, NMET

stages.title: A rupee tomorrow is worth less than a rupee today
stages.text: A mine that returns ₹1000 crore over 30 years can still be a bad investment if most of the money arrives late. | Mining spends heavily up front and earns over decades, so cash flows are discounted: NPV adds them at today's value; IRR is the rate at which NPV is zero. | In India, sales value first pays royalty, plus District Mineral Foundation (DMF) and National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET) contributions calculated on that royalty. | Year-0 capital | Nominal vs discounted | Cumulative discounted cash | NPV & IRR | Why do DMF and NMET depend on royalty? | NPV vs IRR conflicts? | Why discount

title: Grade–Tonnage, Cut-off & Sampling Theory
subtitle: Lane's cut-off and Gy's sampling error

stages.title: Cut-off grade turns rock into ore
stages.text: The same rock is ore at one gold price and waste at another; the cut-off grade draws that line. | The cut-off grade decides which material is ore: raising it shrinks tonnage but raises average grade — the grade–tonnage curve shows the trade. | The break-even cut-off just pays for its own mining and processing; Lane showed that when a capacity is the bottleneck, the optimum cut-off is higher. | Tonnage curve | Grade curve | Break-even cut-off | Chosen cut-off | Lane's three limiting cut-offs? | Gy's sampling theory?

stages.title: The best pit is a closure, not a guess
stages.text: Digging one more rich block can be worth it, or not, depending on how much waste you must strip above it. | Every block gets an economic value: ore blocks earn revenue minus processing and mining; waste blocks only cost mining. | Lerchs–Grossmann finds the set of blocks with maximum total value that respects slope precedence — mining a block requires removing the blocks above it. | Shallow lens | Deep rich pod | Pit outline | Floating cone vs LG? | Nested pits and pushbacks? | Link to BESR?

stages.title: When does the deep pod pay?
Sensors only help if alarms drive action
stages.text: A wall usually warns days before it fails; the radar only saves lives if someone acts on the trend. | Slope stability radar measures wall movement to sub-millimetre precision; accelerating creep shows as inverse velocity falling toward zero at failure. | Fleet management (FMS) dispatch, proximity detection and real-time gas monitoring do the same for haulage and underground air — triage by consequence and time-to-harm. | 1/v readings | Actual failure | Now | Why does 1/v go linear? | FMS dispatch? | Real-time gas telemetry?

unitTitle: Indian Mining Legislation, Safety Management & Rescue
title: Statutory Architecture & Duties
subtitle: Who is responsible for what

stages.title: The law is layered — and so is responsibility
stages.text: When something goes wrong underground, the first question is who was responsible, and the law has already answered it. | The Mines Act 1952 sets principles; the Mines Rules 1955 cover health, welfare and hours; CMR 2017 and MMR 1961 carry the technical safety regulations; DGMS circulars add guidance. The OSH&WC Code 2020 consolidates the Act with other labour laws, with regulations under it carrying this architecture forward. | Owner, agent and manager share responsibility for compliance; each official below them carries specific statutory duties. | Acts / Code | Regulations | DGMS circulars |

title: Degrees of Gassiness & Statutory Air Standards
subtitle: Classification drives precautions

stages.title: How gassy is the seam? The answer sets the rulebook
stages.text: Two seams, same coal: one gives off a little methane, the other a lot, and they are run under different rulebooks. | Coal seams are classified into Degree I, II or III by the rate of methane emission per tonne of coal and the inflammable gas in the general body of air. | Higher degrees bring stricter requirements: flameproof or intrinsically safe apparatus, permitted explosives, more frequent and continuous gas monitoring. | Degree I | Degree II | Degree III | General-body threshold | Statutory air quality? | Statutory air quantity?

title: Risk Management: SMP, HIRA & WRAC
subtitle: From hazard to residual risk

stages.title: Rate the risk, then climb the hierarchy
stages.text: A hazard you cannot remove you can still engineer out, guard against, or train for, and the order matters. | Risk = likelihood × consequence. HIRA identifies hazards and rates them; WRAC (workplace risk assessment and control) does it task by task with the workforce. | The Safety Management Plan (SMP) turns the ranked risks into controls, monitoring and audits — prioritising elimination and engineering over rules and PPE. | Inherent risk | Hierarchy of controls | Consequence axis | Why is PPE last? | What makes an SMP effective?

stages.title: Big disasters need several things to go wrong
stages.text: No single failure caused most mine explosions; gas, ignition and a missed check all had to line up. | A fault tree works backward from a top event through AND and OR gates to basic causes. | An explosion needs a flammable mixture AND an ignition source: attacking either branch cuts the top probability multiplicatively. | Top event | AND gate | OR gate | Basic events | FTA vs ETA vs HAZOP? | Minimal cut sets?

title: Mine Rescue, Breathing Apparatus & First Aid
subtitle: Respiratory physiology and oxygen regeneration

stages.title: A rescuer's mission is measured in litres of oxygen
stages.text: A rescue team's limit is not courage but litres of oxygen; the turn-back point is set before they go in. | Closed-circuit breathing apparatus recycles exhaled air: an alkali canister absorbs CO₂ and a cylinder adds the oxygen the body consumes — about 1 L/min at rest, 3 L/min or more in heavy work. | Duration therefore depends on workload; teams plan travel, work and a reserve, and turn back at a calculated gauge pressure. | Travel in | Reserve | Cylinder | Turn-around pressure | Self-rescuer chemistry? | CO poisoning first aid? | Rescue organisation?
